text: Before any SQL, it's worth drawing out the whole pipeline in plain English, because the mistake behind this chapter's real bug is exactly the kind of thing that's obvious on a whiteboard and easy to miss once you're deep in syntax.

Here's the full shape. The ticketing API exports JSON, landing in a Snowflake stage. A raw table holds that JSON untouched, in a VARIANT column. A Stream sits on that raw table, watching for new rows since it was last read, with no watermark column to manage by hand. A Task wakes up on a schedule, checks whether the Stream actually has new data, and if so, runs a MERGE that writes structured rows into shared tables. Two views sit on top of those tables, one for Finance, one for Support, and Power BI builds a page from each.

That shared foundation is actually two related tables, each built for what it honestly is. ticket_facts holds one row per ticket, reflecting its current status, priority, and category — that's Support's territory. refund_events holds one row per refund event, append-only, because a single ticket could have more than one refund over time — that's Finance's territory. Keeping these conceptually separate now matters later: in Lesson 13, that exact distinction is where this chapter's bug lives.

A Stream never writes anything — it only tracks change. A Task is the only thing that actually runs a MERGE. Keeping that boundary clear matters for troubleshooting later: if a number is wrong, the Stream is never where the bug lives, but the Task — or two Tasks both trying to do the Stream's one job — always is.
